title: Your local shrine
hookLine: a shrine may be closer than you think

lines: A SMALL BROWN SIGN OFF THE HIGHWAY.
cards: Forty minutes up the highway, past a gas station and a feed store, a small brown sign marks a turnoff. A gravel road. A grotto made of fieldstone, with a statue of Mary and rows of candles in red glass.
A rack of rosaries left by people who prayed and went home.
On a weekday afternoon, a retired couple sits on a bench, a man in work boots kneels on the gravel, and a woman reads the handwritten notes tucked into the stones. None of them flew anywhere.
Some drove past it for years before stopping.

teach.h: A PLACE PEOPLE VISIT TO PRAY.
teach.b: First, what a shrine is. The Church's Code of Canon Law defines one simply: a church or other sacred place that the faithful visit on pilgrimage for a particular reason of devotion, with the local bishop's approval.
So a shrine is measured not by size or fame but by prayer: people come on purpose. Then, the oldest pattern. In Genesis, Jacob is running from his brother.
He stops for the night at an ordinary spot, puts a stone under his head, and dreams of a ladder reaching to heaven. He wakes and says, in effect, the Lord was in this place and I didn't know it.
He calls it the house of God, then sets the stone up as a pillar, pours oil on it, and names the place Bethel. He didn't travel to a well-known holy site. He found one on the road he was already on.
Why do local shrines matter? A grand pilgrimage may come once in a lifetime, and some people can never make one: too sick, too poor, too busy caring for someone.

teach.h: A PILGRIMAGE FOR THE REST OF US.
teach.b: A shrine a drive or a bus ride away is a pilgrimage for the rest of us. It can hold a grandparent's devotion, a parish's history, an immigrant community's patron saint, brought from home.

teach.h: ASK THE PARISH OR THE DIOCESE.
teach.b: Your diocese's website or parish office can tell you which shrines are near.

teach.h: THE LORD WAS IN THIS PLACE.
teach.b: Some sit beside a big church; some are a single statue at the edge of a cemetery. The pilgrimage can be an afternoon, and the prayer the same.

how: Catholics visit diocesan and national shrines near home for a day of prayer, Mass and confession; dioceses and parishes list approved shrines and sometimes organize local pilgrimages to them.

games.q: you're Jacob. you wake from a dream of a ladder to heaven, on a stone you used for a pillow. what do you do with the stone?
o: set it up as a pillar, pour oil on it, and name the place.
carry it with you as a keepsake.
games.why: he sets it up as a pillar, pours oil on top, and calls the place Bethel, after saying it is the house of God.

practice: Think of places within an hour of you where people go to pray: a grotto, a statue at a crossroads, a chapel you've driven past, a side altar with candles always lit.
Picture pulling off the road and walking in with a name, a worry or a thank-you. If you pray, offer that intention now and promise to bring it in person; if you don't, just choose the place.

wordCard.voice: Your local shrine. A church or sacred place near you that people visit on pilgrimage, with the bishop's approval. A pilgrimage in an afternoon. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the word the Code of Canon Law uses for a shrine.

carryVoice: Your line: close to home. A shrine doesn't need to be well-known, only prayed in. Rest well.
